title: Voice and Viewpoint
theme: Literary analysis: point of view and the reliability of a narrator
objectives: I can name a narrator's point of view and explain what that narrator can and cannot know.
I can tell a subjective account from an objective one and give a detail that proves it.
I can decide whether a narrator is reliable and explain what clues I used.
I can explain how an author characterizes a person through a narrator's voice.
rationale: This unit turns the year's opening work on tone into literary analysis. Students already hear attitude in a voice; now they ask who is telling the story, what that person can see, and whether the person can be trusted. The ten words cover where a narrator stands (point of view, vantage, omniscient, detached, intimate), how far the account can be trusted (subjective, objective, partial, unreliable), and what an author does with all of it (characterize). Four of the words carry other meanings that students may know (objective as a goal, intimate as a verb, partial as incomplete, vantage in vantage point), so the unit asks students to use context to choose the sense. It closes the grade 7 sequence on tone, evidence, and argument and prepares students to analyze bias and rhetoric in grade 8.

words.def: Knowing everything, including what every character thinks and feels.
words.ex: In the novel, an omniscient narrator reveals the secret fears of every character.
words.ex2: The omniscient voice told readers what the storm would do before the villagers knew.
words.nonExample: A narrator who knows only what one character sees is not omniscient.

apps.academic: An omniscient narrator can move between characters' minds and show events that no single character sees.
apps.spoken: It felt like the narrator was omniscient and knew everyone's secrets.
apps.writing: Use omniscient when a narrator reports the thoughts of more than one character.

words.def: Based on personal feelings or opinions rather than on facts that can be checked.
words.ex: A review that says the movie was boring is subjective, because it depends on the reviewer's taste.
words.ex2: Her subjective account of the race focused on how nervous she felt.

apps.academic: A subjective account tells us how a person felt, which can be valuable evidence of a point of view.
apps.spoken: That's subjective; it depends on what you like.
apps.writing: Label opinions as subjective and support them with details instead of just saying they are true.

cloze.s: Whether pizza is the best food is a ___ question, since it depends on each person's taste.

cloze2.s: The reporter was told to avoid ___ words such as amazing or awful and to stick to the facts.

misuse.s: A subjective statement can always be proven true or false with a ruler or a clock.
misuse.why: A subjective statement depends on feelings, so a ruler or clock cannot prove it.

words.def: Based on facts that can be checked, not on personal feelings.

words.ex2: A judge must be objective and decide a case by the evidence, not by who she likes.

words.def: To describe or show the main qualities of a person or thing.

words.ex2: Critics characterize the film as a gentle comedy about family life.

words.def: Not able to be trusted to be accurate, honest, or complete.
words.ex: The narrator is unreliable because he calls himself brave but runs from every danger.
words.ex2: An unreliable witness may forget details or change the story.
words.nonExample: A narrator who checks every fact and admits mistakes is not unreliable.

misuse.why: Unreliable means not to be trusted, so always telling the whole truth is the opposite.

words.def: Standing apart from the action and showing no strong feeling or involvement.
words.ex: The detached narrator described the accident in calm, short sentences, as though watching from far away.
words.ex2: She remained detached during the argument and did not take either side.
words.nonExample: A narrator who weeps and shouts during every scene is not detached.

apps.academic: A detached tone can make a shocking event feel even more powerful because it shows no emotion.
apps.spoken: He sounded so detached, as if he didn't care.
apps.writing: Use detached for a narrator or tone that keeps its distance from the feelings of the story.

cloze2.s: Watching the storm from a safe window, Lara felt strangely ___ from the chaos in the streets.

misuse.s: The detached narrator burst into tears and begged the characters to listen to him.
misuse.why: Detached means standing apart without strong feeling; bursting into tears is the opposite.

words.def: Very personal and close, as if sharing private thoughts.

senses.def: To hint or suggest something without saying it directly.

words.ex: The diary has an intimate tone, as if the writer were whispering to a close friend.
words.ex2: Only an intimate circle of friends knew about the surprise party.
words.nonExample: A formal speech read to a crowd of strangers is not intimate.

apps.academic: A first-person narrator often creates an intimate feeling by sharing private thoughts with the reader.
apps.spoken: It was a small, intimate dinner with just family.
apps.writing: Use intimate for a voice or setting that feels close and private.

cloze.s: The narrator's ___ voice made readers feel as though she were confiding secrets to them alone.

cloze2.s: The cafe was small and ___, with only six tables and soft light.

misuse.s: An intimate diary entry is one written coldly for strangers about public facts.
misuse.why: Intimate means personal and close, so a cold note for strangers is the opposite.

words.frame: An intimate voice makes the reader feel ___.

words.def: Favoring one side more than another, so not fair or neutral.

senses.def: Not complete; only a part of the whole.
senses.example: We have only a partial list of the guests, so some names are missing.

words.ex: A referee who is partial to the home team cannot judge the game fairly.
words.ex2: The narrator is partial to Dev, so the story leaves out the damage he caused.
words.nonExample: A judge who treats both sides the same way is not partial.

apps.academic: A partial narrator tells the story in a way that favors one character and hides that character's flaws.
apps.spoken: I can't judge this; I'm too partial to my sister.
apps.writing: Use partial for bias toward a side, and write incomplete when you mean not whole.

cloze2.s: Because the writer was ___ to one candidate, the article praised that person's flaws and ignored her rival's strengths.

misuse.s: A partial referee treats both teams fairly and has no favorite.
misuse.why: Partial means favoring one side, so treating both teams fairly is the opposite.

words.def: A position from which something is viewed or understood.
words.ex: From the vantage of the hilltop, we could see the entire village.
words.ex2: From her vantage as a nurse, she saw how the new rule affected patients.
words.nonExample: A tall wall that blocks your view is not a good vantage.

apps.academic: A witness's vantage affects what she could see, so historians ask where each witness stood.
apps.spoken: From my vantage near the back, I couldn't see the stage.
apps.writing: Name the narrator's vantage to explain what the narrator could and could not know.

misuse.why: A vantage is a position from which something is viewed, not a word at the end of a text.

passage.title: Who Took the Last Cookie?
paras: Every story is told from a point of view, the position of the narrator who shows us the events. Imagine a kitchen where the last cookie has vanished, and picture three different narrators describing it. The choice of narrator changes what we know, whom we trust, and even whom we blame.

An omniscient narrator knows everything, including the thoughts of every character. This narrator might tell us that Dev took the cookie because he had skipped lunch, that Maya noticed but stayed quiet, and that their grandfather had planned to give it to the dog. This narrator has the widest vantage on the scene, so readers feel sure they understand it.

A first-person narrator has only one vantage, what he can see from where he stands. If Dev tells the story, we might read, “I honestly thought the cookie was abandoned.” His account is subjective, shaped by his feelings and wishes, and it is also intimate, because we hear his worries and excuses directly. But when the details do not fit, such as crumbs on his sleeve, we may decide that he is unreliable, a narrator we cannot fully trust.

A third kind of narrator is detached, reporting actions without opinion: “Dev stood at the counter. A cookie sat on the plate. Then the plate was empty.” This objective report gives us facts but no feelings, so we must make our own inferences. A narrator can also be partial, favoring one character. If Dev's best friend tells the story, he may leave out the crumbs.

Authors use these choices to characterize people. A narrator who excuses Dev tells us as much about the narrator as about Dev. A careful reader asks three questions: Who is telling this? What can this person see? And what might this person be leaving out?

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word “unreliable” describes a narrator who
choices: tells the story from far above the scene
knows what every character thinks
cannot be fully trusted to give a true or complete account
describes only actions and never feelings
qs.why: The sentence says that when details do not fit, readers may decide the narrator cannot be fully trusted.

qs.q: What does a detached narrator give the reader?
choices: The thoughts of every character
Actions and facts without opinion, leaving the reader to make inferences
A warm account full of excuses
A story told by a character's best friend
qs.why: The detached example reports actions only, and the passage says readers must make their own inferences.

qs.q: Which detail suggests that Dev may be an unreliable narrator?
choices: He tells the story in the first person.
He says he felt worried.
He skipped lunch.
He says the cookie looked abandoned, but there are crumbs on his sleeve.
qs.why: His claim does not match the crumbs, and a mismatch between words and details is a sign of unreliability.

qs.q: Why does the writer say an omniscient narrator has the widest vantage on the scene?
choices: It uses the longest sentences.
It is always the narrator closest to the main character.
It can see every character's thoughts and the whole scene.
It tells the story in the present tense.
qs.why: The omniscient narrator knows everything, including each character's thoughts, so its position covers the most.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The narrator a writer chooses shapes what readers know, whom they trust, and what they conclude.
Cookies are a common theme in stories.
First-person narrators are always honest.
Omniscient narrators are always the best choice.
qs.why: Each narrator type changes what the reader knows or trusts, and the passage ends by teaching readers to ask who is telling and what is left out.

constructed.prompt: Explain how a story about a lost dog changes when it is told by an omniscient narrator instead of by a first-person narrator. Use omniscient, point of view, and vantage.

shows that a first-person narrator has one vantage

look: shows that her words and actions conflict
explains that the author is revealing character through the narrator's voice
constructed.model: The narrator is unreliable because her words do not match her actions. Her claim is subjective, since it is her opinion of herself. The author uses the difference to characterize her as someone who wants to seem braver than she is.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for analyzing who tells a story and how far to trust the telling, read an informational passage that shows three kinds of narrators using one invented event, and write short passages from different points of view. The unit closes the grade 7 vocabulary sequence on tone, evidence, and argument.

notes.va.omniscient.adj: Omniscient is a narrator knowing all characters' thoughts. Do not teach third-person limited unless students raise it. Ask what an omniscient narrator can reveal that a character cannot, and what the risk is for suspense.
notes.va.point-of-view.phr: Point of view has two uses here: the narrator's position (first person, third person) and a person's attitude about an issue. Have students identify the grammatical clues (I, he, she) before they decide how much the narrator knows.
notes.va.subjective.adj: Subjective is based on feelings and is not automatically wrong. A subjective account can be strong evidence of how a person felt. The aim is to label it, not to reject it.
notes.va.objective.adj: Objective as a goal (noun) appears in senses, since students see it on lesson plans. Here the adjective means fact-based. Warn students that no writer is perfectly objective; ask which words in a text reveal a feeling.
notes.va.characterize.v: Characterize needs a specific action or phrase from the text as support. Use a chart with three columns: what the narrator says, what the character does, what others say. The family includes character and characteristic.
notes.va.unreliable.adj: Unreliable is a judgment from evidence, not just a feeling. Require students to find a mismatch: words versus actions, one detail versus another. Model un- plus reliable.
notes.va.detached.adj: Detached is calm, distant, and observing. It does not mean cold or uncaring in every case, since a detached tone can create strong feeling. Contrast with intimate on a ladder.
notes.va.intimate.adj: The adjective means close and personal; the verb sense (to hint) is pronounced differently and shown in senses for recognition. Do not link the adjective to romance; use diary and confiding voices as examples.
notes.va.partial.adj: Two senses in tension: favoring one side (taught) and incomplete (shown in senses). Use the context: partial to a person versus a partial list. The word impartial is the opposite of the first sense.
notes.va.vantage.n: Vantage is the place from which something is seen. The phrase vantage point is common, so connect it. Ask what a narrator at a window, a rooftop, and a basement could each see.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The narrator says, ‘I honestly thought the cookie was abandoned,’ but crumbs are on his sleeve. His account is subjective and intimate because it comes from his feelings, but the mismatch makes him unreliable. The author is using his voice to characterize him as someone who makes excuses.”
discuss: Which narrator would you trust least if the story involved a rivalry, and why?
How does your own point of view affect how you retell something that happened to you?
misconceptions: A first-person narrator is always honest.
An omniscient narrator is the author.
extend: Rewrite a paragraph of a class text from a different point of view and describe what changed.
Choose a short news article and a diary entry about the same event. Label each sentence as objective or subjective.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to sarcastic and earnest from the first unit: ask which narrators sound sarcastic or earnest, and what that shows about their stance. Revisit inference by asking what a detached narrator leaves the reader to infer. Return to these words two days later when analyzing a new passage, again at one week, and in grade 8 when students analyze bias and rhetoric.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: poco confiable (unreliable), distante (detached), perspectiva (vantage), punto de vista, parcial (cognate for the favoring-one-side sense; may also suggest incomplete), objetivo, subjetivo.

Sense boundaries: objective (goal sense in senses), intimate (verb sense in senses, different pronunciation), partial (incomplete sense in senses), point of view (narrative position and personal attitude share one definition).
Terminology: omniscient is taught without third-person limited; confirm that this matches the grade 7 reading curriculum.
Passage is an invented example; the kitchen scene and characters are fictional.
